item.title: Could Psilocybin Help the Brain After Repeated Concussions?
item.description:
Traumatic Brain Injury

Could Psilocybin Help the Brain After Repeated Concussions?

An animal study offers intriguing clues about brain recovery.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Psilocybin reduced brain swelling and restored more normal blood vessel function after concussion.
  • Study shows psilocybin altered brain region communication patterns during rest post-injury.
  • Psilocybin boosted proteins that aid brain cell survival and promote new neural connections.

It might not come as a surprise that repeated mild traumatic brain injuries (rmTBI), such as repeated concussions, could increase a person’s risk of developing brain diseases later in life. Such conditions include dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. Several changes that may occur in the brain help explain this increased risk.

Brengel, Axe, & Maheswari 2026 reported that injuries can lead to ongoing inflammation in the brain, changes in the structure of brain tissue, reduced blood flow, and damage to the protective barrier that normally helps keep harmful substances out of the brain. Such injuries may also make it harder for the brain to clear away unwanted proteins. Over time, the buildup of such proteins and other changes may contribute to gradual damage and loss of brain cells associated with neurodegenerative diseases. What might be surprising to many is exploratory research of a hallucinogen to learn more about how to possibly help those who have experienced psychiatric problems following concussions.

Source: Marco Allegretti/Unsplash

Exploring psilocybin to address brain injury

Brengel, Axe, & Maheswari 2026 suggested that the hallucinogen psilocybin (PSI) could be used to treat brain injury because of its known anti-inflammatory effects. PSI has been studied for its action as a promoter of neuroplasticity (the brain’s remarkable ability to change and reorganize itself throughout life) and cell growth. They were interested in PSI’s potential therapeutic use for various psychiatric disorders such as substance abuse, severe depression, and anxiety.

The researchers' experimental rat study of PSI was done to explore the drug’s use as an intervention following head injury. The injury specifically presented as a swelling of the tissue above the skull (a bump on the head) at the site of impact. Because rats are most active at night, the researchers conducted their experiment during the rats’ normal active period at night. This made the timing of the experience more comparable to studying an injury occurring during the daytime, when humans are typically most active.

Intervention

Researchers administered a 3.0 mg/kg dose of PSI to test for measurable changes in brain activity, which they detected by tracking changes in blood flow and oxygen levels in the animals’ brains. The researchers tested this dose of PSI using a method that produced repeated mild head injuries to the rats, without breaking or penetrating the skulls, like what happens with repeated concussions for humans. The animals were impacted once each day for three consecutive days.

What the evidence revealed

The findings suggest that psilocybin may help the injured brain in several ways. It reduced swelling caused by fluid leaking into brain tissue and helped blood vessels return to more normal functioning. It also changed patterns of communication among brain regions when the brain was at rest. In addition, psilocybin reduced the buildup of an abnormal form of tau, a protein associated with brain degeneration, and increased levels of proteins that help brain cells survive, adapt, and form new connections. The treatment also affected neurons' fat-based signaling molecules, playing a role in how brain cells communicate and respond to injury.

Takeaways

The researchers stated that there is no approved medical treatment for repeated mild traumatic brain injuries. However, taken together, these findings suggest an intriguing possibility: psilocybin may do more after a brain injury than temporarily alter consciousness, a primary topic of investigation of the substance's psychological effect. We know that inferring findings based on animal studies is not an exact one-to-one relevance to humans' experiences. Yet given the number of injuries humans sustain from repeated bumps to the head in organized sports and accidents, it is helpful to now learn that PSI may influence some of the biological processes involved in the brain’s ability to protect, repair, and reorganize itself.

item.title: Why We Ignore Warning Signs Until It’s Too Late
item.description:
Decision-Making

Why We Ignore Warning Signs Until It’s Too Late

Lessons from the White House Situation Room on overcoming normalcy bias.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Normalcy bias leads us to assume the future will resemble the past, so we explain away warning signs.
  • Deciding in advance "if this happens, then I'll act" can help distinguish crisis from normalcy.
  • Pre-mortems and a designated devil's advocate surface problems while there's still time to fix them.

Growing up, my family faced considerable financial strain. I would overhear my parents worry that our credit card payments were delayed, but out of a desire to stay upbeat, we never spoke about it.

Like many families facing similar challenges, we remained in denial and reassured each other: “We’ll catch up next month.”

It’s an understandable instinct. But the warning signs kept adding up until a true crisis hit. We were turned down for a home loan.

Looking back, what we were missing wasn’t effort or love. It was a moment when someone, any of us, felt able to say what no one wanted to hear: “I know this is hard to discuss, but our spending is unsustainable.”

Instead, we assumed things would work out because, until then, they usually had. That isn’t unique to my family. It’s a common pattern in human thinking.

Psychologists call this normalcy bias, the tendency to assume that things will continue as they always have and that the future won’t diverge too far from what we expect.

You probably have some examples in your own life — a relationship you couldn’t accept was falling apart, or a shrinking job market you swore couldn’t affect you. Our brains favor familiar patterns and struggle to simulate extreme disruptions.

We assume that if something hasn’t happened before, it probably won’t happen now. And when a threat persists over time without causing direct personal harm, we can begin to normalize it.

So how do we counter normalcy bias before a problem becomes impossible to ignore?

Decide in advance when to act

When I served at the White House National Security Council helping create the nation’s playbook for dangerous health emergencies, my team used objective “if/then” triggers. If a certain threshold was crossed, then we acted.

If a case of polio appeared in a region where it had previously been eliminated, or reports emerged of an unusual strain of influenza, then we would ask the White House Situation Room to convene a government-wide team to rapidly assess the incident.

The point was to have an objective measure to guide us rather than relying only on how alarming a situation felt in the moment.

I saw the value of this approach in 2023, when I received notice from the Situation Room that an unusual strain (H5N1) of influenza had infected a father and killed his daughter in a remote Cambodian village. A new pandemic influenza could infect and kill millions.

The National Security Advisor asked me, “Do we need to brief President Biden immediately?”

First, we needed to determine whether we had seen telltale signs of a pandemic, such as sustained human-to-human transmission of respiratory disease.

Working with the CDC, WHO, and local health officials, we looked at hospital surveillance data on influenza-like illnesses near the village and compared it with previous years. Cases were not unexpectedly higher, so we were reassured.

We didn’t have to alert the President yet. But we had an objective measure we could continue to monitor in case the situation changed.

In the Situation Room, if/then triggers reduced decision delay and our bias toward maintaining the status quo. They also helped counter overreaction: our sense that things were “under control” had some basis in objective information, not just on hope.

The same approach can be useful outside government. An if/then trigger gives you a specific point at which you’ve decided to reassess a situation or take action, rather than continuing to tell yourself that things are probably fine.

The trigger might be financial, health-related, or something at work. What matters is deciding on it in advance, when you’re less likely to rationalize a warning sign.

Test your assumptions

My National Security Council team and I also used two other techniques to reduce overconfidence: simulations and red teaming.

Simulations: To prepare for future pandemics, we ran “pre-mortems” and scenario simulations. Like military officials preparing for conflicts, we ran exercises with senior government leaders to simulate influenza and other respiratory pandemic scenarios.

We would convene government officials, disease detectives, and emergency responders to walk through a realistic scenario in which a new infectious disease began to spread. Over time, participants would receive pieces of information: rising hospital cases, shortages of supplies, or new variants.

Then they had to decide what to do. When should we issue warnings? How would we protect hospitals? When would we consider closing schools or businesses?

The goal was to stress-test our plans and determine where decisions might get delayed and what might break as a threat worsened. This helped us find flaws while there was still time to fix them.

Pre-mortems: A simulation plays a scenario forward. A pre-mortem works in reverse. I’ve seen this work in companies. When I oversaw software teams preparing to launch a major update to digital education apps for health workers, optimism could create its own form of groupthink. Everyone wanted the launch to succeed, and critical voices might hold back from mentioning potential bugs or server issues.

A pre-mortem simulation asked the team to visualize that the launch had already failed and ask, "What went wrong?" That could help coworkers spot red flags and address them before the software update rolled out.

You can apply this in your own life. Think of a pre-mortem as a low-stakes rehearsal for stress; a way to practice how you respond before a real crisis hits. Ask yourself: “It’s a year from now and I’ve lost my job. What went wrong? Did I have a financial buffer? Who did I call for help?”

Red teaming: In the Situation Room, we also used “red teaming,” a practice used by U.S. intelligence officials in which someone is assigned to take the contrarian position and assess what could go wrong.

You can apply this principle in your family or community by designating a “devil’s advocate.” The role of the devil’s advocate, like “red teams” reviewing Situation Room crisis playbooks, is to offer dissent, helping to detect problems earlier and make better decisions in uncertainty. Before a big decision, ask: “Who has permission to disagree, and have we heard from them yet?”

That is what my family was missing. We didn’t need more optimism. What we needed was someone willing to voice structured dissent, like a red-team member in the Situation Room, to disrupt our denial and push us to act before the situation became unmanageable.

From denial to action

As I learned in researching and writing my new book, Safer: A Playbook – Turning Fear into Action and Crisis into Community, normalcy bias is most dangerous in a slow-moving crisis, when each warning sign looks small on its own and “we’ll catch up next month” sounds reasonable every single month.

If/then triggers, pre-mortems, and red teaming won’t make the hard conversations easy. But they make it possible to move from fear and denial into action.

item.title: Is There Such a Thing as an Addictive Personality?
item.description:
Addiction

Is There Such a Thing as an Addictive Personality?

An alleged personality type purports to explain compulsive behaviors.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Some people who do not drink claim to have an "alcoholic's" or "addictive" personality.
  • Addictive personality is not a recognized medical condition.
  • The argument about addictive personalities rests on unjustified assumptions and reinforces stereotypes.
  • Moral philosophy offers a richer approach to explaining and evaluating behavior.

Can a person who has never drunk in troubling or addictive ways have an “alcoholic’s personality"? Does such a thing even exist? What role does it play in explaining anyone else’s behavior?

The expression “alcoholic’s personality” has been in the news recenty because Susie Wiles, President Trump’s Chief of Staff, said in an interview with Vanity Fair magazine that President Trump has it. She claimed, “high-functioning alcoholics or alcoholics in general, their personalities are exaggerated when they drink. And so I’m a little bit of an expert in big personalities.”

She adds that Trump believes that “there’s nothing he can’t do. Nothing, zero, nothing.” Wiles acknowledges that the experience she brings to bear on the matter comes from her late father, former professional football player and commentator, Pat Summerall, who had lived with alcoholism.

Trump agreed with Wiles’s assessment after it became public. He stated in the New York Post that “I’m fortunate I am not a drinker. If I did, I could very well, because I’ve said that—what’s the word? Not possessive—possessive and addictive type personality. Oh, I’ve said it many times, many times before.”

Addictive personalities

The expression “addictive personality” is more commonly used than “alcoholic’s personality,” but they share ancestry although neither is a recognized medical condition. An addictive personality is generally understood to be a constellation of psychological characteristics, health conditions, and environmental factors.

An addictive personality comprises a range of traits and behaviors including impulsivity, risk-taking, thrill-seeking, overindulgence, difficulty in self-regulation, preferring short-term benefits over long-term ones, engaging in obsessive or compulsive behaviors, difficulty in accepting limitations or constraints, and unwillingness to take responsibility. Some might also include comfort with lying and deception. These traits allegedly explain why some people develop an addiction.

In a significant sense, addiction gets defined by these traits regardless of any substances used, including alcohol, cocaine, and heroin, or behaviors such as gambling, scrolling TikTok for hours, etc. Thus, it's understandable for Wiles to say it about President Trump and for him to agree, but this is an argument that needs to be unpacked because it is has several logical and practical flaws.

Flaws in the argument about addictive personalities

The first significant flaw of the argument is the reliance on a generalization. For a generalization to be justified, it must be based on a large representative sample. Wiles’s generalization is based on a very small and not representative sample pool. Very familiar stereotypes do the heavy lifting in her generalization, which in turn reinforce the stereotypes taken as evidence. For example, many alcoholics or addicts do not believe there is nothing they can’t do.

The second issue with Wiles’s argument, and the media’s parroting of it, is the reliance on circular characterization. Here’s the circle: If one has all or most of these traits, one has an addiction, and having an addiction means one has all or most of the traits. Stereotypes and their use in unjustified generalizations are taken as evidence of the circular relationship.

An argument that goes in circles is an instance of begging the question, the third flaw in the argument. An argument that begs the question is one in which a premise of the argument assumes the truth of the conclusion. Someone who claims, “Wilson tennis balls are superior to Penn because they have Wilson’s fiber technology,” begs the question. They don’t offer actual evidence for the superiority of Wilson’s technology, which would support the claim they’re the better tennis ball. This circular characterization is simply assumed in the relationship between “addictive personality” and “addiction.” This assumption needs much more evidence than it presently has.

Such arguments can lead to harmful conclusions in the real world. “Addictive personality” sounds like an objective condition, but it may be a dangerous fiction as it creates and reinforces stereotypes that serve as the basis for generalizations that then pass as medical or common knowledge. The circle just gets more vicious.

What moral philosophy offers

There is no need to invoke the fiction of an addictive or alcoholic personality to morally explain and evaluate someone’s behavior. We have plenty of concepts from a variety of moral traditions that should be used instead. We might look to Aristotle and Confucius, who focus on virtue and character, arguing that we become who we are by what we do repeatedly. Present acts spring from a moral character formed over a lifetime.

Immanuel Kant offers the categorical imperative. One formulation is: Never act in such a way that we treat humanity, whether in ourselves or in others, as a means only but always as an end in itself. In other words, don’t use people and treat them as pawns for your own benefit or enrichment, but rather act in ways that respect others’ autonomy and dignity. Rights, fairness, impartiality, and equality have their genesis in this tradition.

We can draw from relationship ethics that prioritize healthy and respectful relations with ourselves and other humans near and far, as well as with animals and the Earth itself. Relationship ethics asks us how to think about our inalienable responsibilities to these others.

Ascribing someone’s behaviors to an addictive personality is far too easy to do because it functions as shorthand. We need to use rich, varied, and complex moral concepts to explain and evaluate behavior instead.

item.title: Jazz as Storytelling
item.description:
Positive Psychology

Jazz as Storytelling

Improvisational jazz is a conversational story between players and audience.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Both jazz and stories evoke strong emotions and feelings of connection.
  • Both stories and music create interpersonal brain synchronization, syncing our brains.
  • The meaning of stories and of jazz shifts with each retelling.

Jazz is a story. Not all stories are told in words; they are also told in emotion, communication, cadence, and rhythm. Jazz is a story told between and among people, involving improvised riffs, questions and answers, and call and response. Jazz touches our souls and syncs our brains.

Last night I was privileged to hear a remarkable story told between father and son, an intergenerational jazz story. Kenny Banks Sr. and Jr., both accomplished jazz pianists, sat together on the same piano bench at Churchill Downs, an elegant reincarnation of a revered Atlanta jazz club that just opened in Decatur, GA. The sheer exuberance, joy, and love that emerged from their performance were breathtaking. Through their musical exchange, they told a story of their relationship, both to the music and to each other. Why is music, and especially jazz, so powerfully evocative?

I often write about the power of storytelling, and especially how family storytelling, sharing and listening, is foundational both for the family as a whole and for each individual family member in building a sense of identity, meaning, and purpose in life. Importantly, it is not the story itself, but the telling and sharing. Certainly, knowing family histories and having stories of trials and triumphs of generations past matters; these stories provide the ground from which resilience grows. But it is the active, living stories, the sitting down together, the asking and the answering, the changing bits and pieces that come into focus, the meanings that shift and fall into place, as we share the stories together.

Sharing stories in this way has physical consequences. When we share stories, we show what is called “interbrain synchronization”— the storyteller and listener’s brains actually align, showing the same activation patterns as the story unfolds, and, as Xie and colleagues have shown, this may be a stronger effect for happy than for sad stories. Stories, quite literally, connect us.

Music, and particularly improvisational jazz, connects us in much the same way. Whereas all music, like all stories, creates emotional resonance and meaning, improvisational jazz creates a conversation, both between the players and between the players and the audience. Bob Reynolds, writing about jazz, explains the rule of three: just like stories, jazz begins with a statement, moves into a response (the development of a new idea, introducing tension), and arrives at a destination, a cohesive conclusion. Jazz is a narrative arc.

Kenny Banks Sr. and Jr. have told this story before—the piece they played was clearly well-known and well-loved. But in this moment, they created something new, a new response, a new interpretation, a new way of sharing the story. This is what we do as storytellers all the time. Storytelling is not static but changes depending on the teller, the listener, the reasons for sharing. It is this aspect of family storytelling that makes it so powerful—it adapts to the moment. As does jazz.

Jazz has a long history intertwined with political, economic, and historical factors that defined a genre and an identity. Just as family stories build resistance and strength, so does jazz. Sharing jazz across the generations, telling stories that might only be able to be told through music, as no words can express it, jazz creates an emotional resonance that connects us all, family to family, neighbor to neighbor, person to person. Listening to live improvisational jazz is a privilege and a pleasure. And to listen in on the creation of such a beautiful intergenerational story told through jazz was amazing.

item.title: Why Can't I Look Away?
item.description:
Anxiety

Why Can't I Look Away?

The psychology of our fascination with tragedy.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Fascination with tragedy is a normal threat-learning response, not a character flaw.
  • Unresolved cases hold our attention longest because the mind keeps working on open questions.
  • When following a story stops informing you and starts activating you, it’s time to change how you consume it.
Why Can't I Look Away: Part I
Source: Whitney Coulson

This post is part 1 in a series.

This year, a few stories have taken over our feeds, our group chats, our dinner tables, and, more often than I expected, my therapy office.

In Massachusetts, the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse who killed her three young children, ended in a mistrial in September after jurors couldn’t agree on whether she was criminally responsible.

In New York, a lawsuit alleges that seven Cornell University fraternity members sexually assaulted a fellow student in 2024. The accused, dubbed the “Cornell 7” online, deny criminal responsibility, and the investigation has since been reopened.

In Mississippi, 18-year-old Nolan Wells went to Horn Island with friends on the Fourth of July and never came home. Months later, his family is still searching for answers. So is the family of Daniel Erving, an 18-year-old in Texas who drowned in April after jumping into a lake with two companions, both of whom are now charged with tampering with evidence.

Sadly, none of these stories is the first of its kind. Andrea Yates’s trial put postpartum psychosis in front of a jury more than two decades ago. A case at Stanford turned a campus sexual assault into a national argument in 2016. And the question of whether a young Black man’s death will be honestly investigated is one Mississippi, and the country, has been asking since Emmett Till. What’s different now is how fast, how loudly, and how personally these stories reach us.

Each involves real people and real grief, and the way we connect to them runs along a spectrum, from curiosity to fascination—and for some of us, all the way to activation. For many of my clients, staying informed has come at the cost of nervous system dysregulation, and finding their way back to baseline has taken real therapeutic work.

In this series, I’ll look at each case through a different psychological lens. But first, the question I hear constantly from clients, colleagues, and friends: Why can’t I stop watching?

Reason One: Your Brain Is Practicing for Danger

If you’ve found yourself deep in the rabbit hole, following every new detail with a commitment that goes well beyond curiosity, you are not alone. Researchers have a name for this pull—morbid curiosity—and they describe it as an ordinary human trait. Coltan Scrivner and colleagues propose that our draw toward frightening events helps us learn about threats from a safe distance. When we read about a tragedy, part of the mind is quietly running a simulation: How did this happen? What were the signs? Could this happen to me, or to my kids?

That’s why the details we fixate on tend to be so practical: Who was there? Who knew? Why didn’t anyone call? Underneath those questions is a mind trying to build a map of danger, driven by something as old as we are: self-preservation.

Reason Two: We Struggle With Unfinished Business

In the 1920s, psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik observed that people tend to remember interrupted tasks better than completed ones. The broader idea, that unfinished business keeps tugging at us, goes a long way toward explaining why these particular stories have such a hold. This is similar to why we replay events in our head, such as breakups, when we feel we are missing important details. We seek closure.

None of these stories has an ending. A jury that couldn’t reach a unanimous verdict. An investigation reopened. A family still waiting to learn how their son died. When a story stays open, the mind keeps circling back, refreshing the feed in case the answer has finally arrived. It’s the same pull that keeps us watching a TV series after a cliffhanger, and the media knows it well.

Reason Three: We See Ourselves in the Details

A tragedy becomes personal when we can see ourselves, or someone we love, inside it. A mother who seemed to be functioning. A college student at a party. A teenager on a summer trip with friends. Nothing about these circumstances is extraordinary. They map right onto ordinary life, and that ordinariness is exactly what makes them so frightening. The feeling of association is what keeps us engaged.

Reason Four: The Content Never Stops

How we take in these stories has changed, too. Courtroom livestreams, recap videos, theories, and memes show up within hours of every development. The algorithm rewards what’s most emotional, not what’s most accurate. And picking a side offers something a lot of us crave: a community of people who feel the way we do.

The cost of all this is easy to miss. After the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing, researchers found that people who took in six or more hours of coverage a day in the week that followed reported more acute stress than some people who were actually at the scene. Repeated exposure doesn’t just inform our threat system; it can keep it switched on.

From Informed to Activated

A few signs that following a case has shifted from informing you to activating you:

  • You keep scrolling even though you feel worse each time.
  • You’re sleeping less, or replaying details at night.
  • You feel irritable, numb, or on edge in situations that have nothing to do with the case.
  • Comment-section arguments feel personal and are hard to shake.
  • You’re checking for updates compulsively, even when you know there aren’t any.

None of this means something is wrong with you. Your attention is doing exactly what it evolved to do, but you get to choose how you feed it. Try setting a defined window for news, muting keywords for a few days, or reading one reliable summary instead of watching the clips. And talk with someone you trust about what’s coming up for you.

Future posts in this weekly series will focus on the Lindsay Clancy trial, the Cornell case, and the sons who didn't come home.

If you’re struggling, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: 8 Questions to Transform Your Adult Child-Parent Connection
item.description:
Family Dynamics

8 Questions to Transform Your Adult Child-Parent Connection

Grown children have the power to address challenges in their bond with parents.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • You must first have a clear-eyed view of your relationship with a parent before you can make improvements.
  • Parents’ individual backgrounds often hold the key to annoying patterns affecting you as a grownup.
  • Committing to improving your relationship liberates you from your “child” role and can reduce conflict.
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

Grown-up relationships with parents are layered and complex, and at times, frustrating and stressful. The good news is that it is possible to make meaningful improvements in how you relate to your parents as an adult if you start from a place of understanding.

You may feel at a loss about how to change the situation because this relational dynamic has existed to some extent since you were a young child. So the first step to turning around adult child-parent issues is identifying and defining those challenges. Contrary to what you may believe, you have clear options—and many more than you may think—to direct the course of your connection, including with the most difficult parents.

By contrast, when problems are allowed to fester, they can threaten the adult child-parent relationship. For example, if parents try to exert power over grown children, that can put strain on the relationship that erupts into arguments and even possibly estrangement.

Years ago, while doing research for my book, Nobody’s Baby Now: Reinventing Your Adult Relationship with Your Mother and Father, I wondered why every family doesn’t strive for an equitable balance of power once the children are adults. We tend to hold on to old childhood patterns because it seems too difficult to rectify them. How do you change an intrusive mother or domineering father, a manipulative parent, or one who must be “right” whatever the situation?

But small improvements can go a long way to mend your connection or at least avoid harmful interactions.

Questions to Ask Yourself

Before you can move to a closer, more comfortable, and rewarding bond with a parent, you need to recognize where it is now and what upsets you the most. Answering these questions will allow you to pinpoint problem areas and prioritize what you need to address first.

  • Does the relationship feel balanced to you?
  • Do you feel your parents expect too much from you?
  • Are your parents too involved in your life or too demanding of your time?
  • Do they influence your thinking too much?
  • Do you and they communicate too often or too infrequently?
  • Are boundaries clearly defined and understood?
  • Do your parents respect your feelings?
  • Do you tense up or feel guilty when you hear your parent’s voice?

Your responses to the questions above will help you create a roadmap outlining which problem areas to tackle so you feel less annoyed or stressed. Even if you believe your parent can’t or won’t change, there’s room for small alterations to ease resentment or at least become more tolerant of a parent’s irksome behavior or attitude.

Starter Tweaks and Insights

Once you better understand what you want to address, it’s time to turn your attention to how you can influence or achieve change. The dynamic between you wasn’t created overnight, and rapid, sweeping change isn’t likely. Rather, the goal should be meaningful, smaller improvements that add up over time.

The following are a few examples of where you might start. The actions you take, of course, depend on what you see as the difficulties.

  • If you feel guilty when you hear your parent’s voice, recognize that there is a fine line between guilt-driven obligation to a person and genuine desire to be in contact. Strive for real connection that makes you want to stay in touch and be with or hear from your parents. Focus on a common interest—politics, cooking, gardening, the grandchildren—and steer conversations back to your shared “safe” topics.
  • If a parent is trying to run your life, figure out where you can cut back interactions or offer less information about what is going on. Maintain the relationship at the level you feel comfortable with rather than simply responding to unrealistic demands.
  • Calmly tell a parent when you feel they are being too controlling, critical, or demanding. You might say, “Dad, it makes me feel as if I’m 10 years old when you say [fill in the blank with what problematic thing(s) that parent says] or tell me what to do.”
  • Be aware of what you want and need from your parent and what they are capable of or prepared to do.

By addressing the issues you identify, you’ll become less susceptible to what upsets you and more open to a closer tie. You may not be able to “fix” everything you see as troublesome, but with small changes accumulating over time, you can improve your bond and draw closer.

item.title: Speaking in Tongues
item.description:
Cognition

Speaking in Tongues

The surprising connections between language and food.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Food words provide clues to linguistic and cultural history.
  • Grammar rules can change when the subject is food.
  • How foods are described can impact how they taste—but not always.

October isn’t just for pumpkin spice lattes. It’s for all kinds of foods and beverages. October 16 is World Food Day, October 24 is National Food Day, and there are lots of other food days besides these two all-encompassing “holidays,” from National Homemade Cookies Day on October 1 (yum!) to National Chocolate-Covered Insects Day on October 14 (yuck!).

Besides such labels marking food days, there are many other connections between language and food. In fact, there’s a whole subfield of linguistics, the scientific study of human language, devoted to this topic—"culinary linguistics.”

Shared Food Words, Shared Linguistic Heritage

Why would linguists want to study language and food? For one, food terms shed light on the history of languages and peoples. If the same word or related words for a particular food or drink are found across different languages, then that may be a clue that there was once a common ancestral language—or that one common source had significant influence.

For example, “coffee,” from Arabic “qahwah,” can be traced from Ethiopia to Turkey to countries and languages throughout Europe and beyond. Similarly, the word “curry” traveled from South India across the globe via Portuguese and English traders as the spicy food, in its many variations, became popular beyond its original borders.

Curry
Source: Andy Hay / Unsplash

Cultural Contact and Linguistic Borrowings

Food words also yield insight into historical patterns of contact. The Latinate words “butter” and “cheese” were adopted into English long before the Norman Conquest of England in 1066. This shows that Brits had regular relations with speakers of Romance languages like Latin and French prior to this historic date (which makes sense given that there was substantial Roman occupation of Britain for centuries).

Other borrowings show just how quickly foreign words can be nativized when tasty food items are involved: The French word “Camembert” is widespread in English but didn’t enter the language until 1878. And, believe it or not, the now ubiquitous Italian word (and food) “spaghetti” didn’t enter the common parlance among English speakers until 1845.

The Syntax of “Food Speak”

Linguists, being the selfish creatures they are, are also interested in language and food for the insights this line of study offers us into the boundaries of language itself. Specialized registers like those used for recipes and menus shed light on how far a given language can stretch its grammar and still be considered acceptable. “Mix well and fold into flour mixture” sounds fine in the recipe context, but in other settings, it would be odd to not indicate just what you’re mixing.

Native speakers of English also don’t often leave out “the” before nouns like “flour mixture”—unless, again, we’re talking “Recipe English.”

Posh vs. Pedestrian Foods

Words for foods also lend insight into social structure: When the French conquered the English in the Medieval days, they brought in their posh words for fancy cooked foods served “above stairs” to contrast with the old Anglo-Saxon terms for live animals on the hoof—“beef’ vs. “cow,” “mutton” vs. “sheep,” and “pork” vs. plain old “pig.”

And the adjectives used to describe foods are also revealing. For example, one study found that labels on more expensive bags of potato chips use more complex language and fancier adjectives (such as “fluorescent” and “flair”) and also emphasize qualities like healthiness and naturalness. Less expensive chips are described in simpler terms (“fresh and light”) and are praised for their “authenticity.”

Taste Buds vs. Native Tongues

Garlic and onions
Source: Andreas ***** / Unsplash

And then there’s the question of whether words related to foods and flavors actually influence our taste buds: Do speakers of languages with fewer words for tastes experience less taste differentiation? Can I train my taste buds to make finer distinctions by studying specialized vocabulary (like the intricate language of wine tasting)? After all, research has shown that vision and hearing are impacted by language, so shouldn’t we expect taste to behave the same?

It turns out that the answer is sometimes yes, but sometimes no.

One study showing this less-than-straightforward connection between language and taste involved native speakers of English vs. Norwegian. In English, the words for two related foods, “onion” and “garlic” (both with very strong flavors), are completely different. In Norwegian, the words are related—“onion” is “lök,” and garlic is “vitlök”—literally “white onion.” We might expect, therefore, that Norwegian speakers performing a (blind) taste test would group “onion” and “garlic” as tasting more alike than would speakers of English.

Instead, after tasting each food, both speaker groups classified onion and garlic as distinctive flavors. This shows that when there’s direct evidence from taste buds, language does not override taste sensations.

However, when similar tests are performed using just pictures or food names alone, with no actual tasting, then we do see language effects. Speakers of Mandarin Chinese rate “yīngtáo” (cherry) and “táozi” (peach) as very different flavors when they taste juices made from these fruits. But when study participants are only shown pictures, they group the two as similar, likely because both labels contain “táo.”

Similarly, English speakers rate “grape” and “grapefruit” as similar when looking at pictures vs. tasting, and they do the same with “apple” and “pineapple,” despite their very different tastes.

In other words, when no taste buds are involved, language actually can impact what we think things taste like

Language and Taste Expectations

Finally, food terms impact our taste perceptions by coloring our expectations. “Smoked salmon frozen savory mousse” tastes better to research participants (and lights up different brain receptors) than the same product labeled “smoked salmon ice cream.” Apparently, we don’t like dissonance between savory and sweet, especially when a label primes us to expect a sweet treat when the actual taste is something else. When it comes to language and food, it looks like we all have a sweet tooth!

Food for Thought…

While you won’t find “smoked salmon ice cream day” on the October food calendar (thankfully!), there are lots of other food-related days—and words—to savor, from Meatloaf Appreciation Day (October 18) to National Pumpkin Cheesecake Day (October 21). And don’t forget the linguists’ favorite: October 9 is “Submarine Hoagie Hero Grinder Day,” celebrating not only the specialty sandwich but the rich array of dialect words Americans use to describe it. Bon appétit!

item.title: Why Do ADHD Stimulants Wear Off Early, and What Can Be Done?
item.description:
ADHD

Why Do ADHD Stimulants Wear Off Early, and What Can Be Done?

From unique ADHD med metabolism to daily demands, one size does not fit all.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • ADHD stimulant medications can have different duration of action in different children.
  • Medications are made to last a certain time, but that can still vary from child to child.
  • Factors like age and daily demands will impact medication planning .
  • Just because it's a long-acting medication doesn't mean it will last long enough.

All People With ADHD Are Not Alike

There’s a popular saying in the clinical world: “If you’ve met one person with ADHD, you’ve met one person with ADHD.” Every individual’s ADHD and their medication responses present uniquely to their brain and body. I was reminded of this recently over the course of a single day in my office as several patients and families described their experiences with stimulants—and the stark contrast in their stories caught my attention.

Consider these real-world examples from my practice:

The 1st Grader: Their extended-release Focalin (dexmethylphenidate ER) wore off by lunchtime, requiring a second mid-day dose.

The Young Adult: A single short-acting Focalin (dexmethylphenidate) in the morning lasted all day. Taking it any later meant tossing and turning all night.

The High Schooler: Once thrived on Vyvanse’s (lisdexamfetamine) all-day benefit, but suddenly found it fizzling out after just four hours.

The 8th Grader: As coursework intensified, their long-acting Concerta (methylphenidate ER) needed a late-afternoon Ritalin (methylphenidate short-acting) “booster” just to get through homework.

Source: Pixel Shot / Shutterstock

The Building Blocks: Formulations and Duration

ADHD stimulants fall into two main chemical families: methylphenidate-based (like Ritalin and Focalin) and amphetamine-based (like Adderall and Vyvanse). Beyond basic chemical formulas, the options vary by two primary levers:

Formulation (how it gets into the body and how it’s taken): Tablets, capsules, liquids, chewables, or transdermal skin patches.

Duration (how long it lasts in the body before being eliminated): Immediate-release (short-acting, 3–6 hours) versus extended- or sustained-release (long-acting, 6–13 hours).

Even within these categories, response curves vary dramatically. Here are the key factors clinicians evaluate when tailoring a stimulant regimen:

Factors Affecting a Child’s Medication Needs and Responses

1. Age and School Demands: A single long-acting dose helps students avoid trips to the nurse’s office. For preschoolers, short-acting options are typically trialed first for safety, though severe symptoms impacting home life may warrant longer coverage.

2. Homework and After-School Demands: Long-acting meds often wear off right as sports, clubs, or heavy homework loads begin. A carefully timed afternoon booster can bridge the gap without disrupting sleep.

3. Daily Routines: Consistent wake-up times favor long-acting options. However, teens sleeping in on weekends may experience insomnia if they take an extended-release dose late in the day.

4. Appetite Suppression: If a long-acting stimulant ruins a child’s appetite at lunch, switching to a short-acting dose in the morning may help them eat something before taking a second dose that will reduce appetite again.

5. Medication Profiles: Not all long-acting meds are created equal. Focalin (dexmethylphenidate) XR often acts like a “medium-range” option, whereas Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine) or Concerta (methylphenidate ER) can provide 8 to 10+ hours of coverage—though clinical benefits usually soften before the drug fully clears the system.

6. Individual Medication Metabolism (How Fast the Body Breaks Down the Medication): Metabolic rates can differ dramatically. Vyvanse might last 10 hours for one child and five for another. Even if you have genetic testing that provides an idea of the child’s medication metabolism profile, trial-and-error remains essential.

7. Shifts Over Time: Effectiveness can change due to growth, new generic formulations, or routine shifts. Adjustments are a normal part of long-term care.

8. The Transdermal Patch Alternative: Skin patches offer exceptionally steady absorption and bypass the digestive tract entirely. Plus, removing the patch roughly an hour before bedtime helps you have full control over duration of action. However, ongoing supply shortages remain a challenge to prescribing the patches.

Source: Media_Photos / Shutterstock

The Takeaway

There’s a common misconception that a single long-acting pill should cover an entire day. In reality, many patients benefit from a tailored approach—combining extended coverage with an afternoon booster or scaffolded regimen. Working collaboratively with your doctor ensures maximum symptom control with minimal side effects.

For prescribers, we need to focus on listening actively to the concerns of our patients and their parents to make sure we are hearing the stories of their individual days—and not what we expect to happen based on our expectations for the medication or what other patients have experienced.

Remember

I am a child and adolescent psychiatrist, but probably not yours or your child’s. This post is for informational purposes only. Be sure to discuss your child’s stimulant prescriptions with your prescriber. I hope this gives you some ideas about questions to ask and information to share. Never make any changes to medications without consulting your doctor.

item.title: Don’t Try to Understand Everything
item.description:
Career

Don’t Try to Understand Everything

Embrace uncertainty and give new ideas time before rushing to judge them.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Tolerating uncertainty rather than rushing to judgment allows complex, innovative ideas time to develop.
  • Cognitive closure drives us to seek instant answers, often making us dismiss novel concepts prematurely.
  • Communicating through emotion and experience is just as valuable as using data and logical explanations.
  • Approaching unfamiliar challenges with curiosity rather than a need for control yields better results.

When I visited the Venice Biennale this summer, I felt puzzled by most of the art I saw. Most of us ask ourselves, “What does this mean?”—not just with art, but with many things in life and work. We want to work things out right away, but that can lead us astray. Sometimes, it’s better to wait before judging something new.
For example, when I walked through Lubaina Himid’s exhibition in the British Pavilion, I was drawn in by the lively colours, energy, and bold brushstrokes in her paintings. Still, I felt confused by what the figures were doing and by the symbols on the sides. I tried to work them out. What were the figures doing? What did the symbols mean? What was Himid trying to say?

This is something we all experience. I didn’t understand something right away, so my mind wanted to solve the mystery. I looked for an answer before I had really spent time with the art.

Lubaina Himid exhibition
Source: Rod Judkins

The Psychology of “Negative Capability”

In psychology, the urge to quickly resolve uncertainty is called cognitive closure. When things get complicated, our minds hurry to make decisions so we can feel more at ease.

The Romantic poet John Keats described the opposite approach as Negative Capability. This means being able to tolerate uncertainty, mystery, and doubt without always needing clear facts or reasons. As Keats wrote, it is the ability to remain in “uncertainties, Mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact & reason.”

If we try to understand things too quickly, we often use old ways of thinking for new ideas. New ideas can seem confusing or even wrong at first. If we look for certainty right away, we might reject things just because we don’t get them yet. Practicing “Negative Capability” helps us give ideas time to show their value before we judge them.

This is what happened to me with Himid’s paintings. My first reaction was to try to work them out. I wanted to know what they meant before I let myself just experience them. But the paintings spoke to me before I understood their message. I noticed the colour, movement, energy, and emotion before I understood what the figures were doing or what the symbols meant. Sometimes, our urge to explain things gets in the way of really experiencing them. To understand Himid’s art, or anything new, you need to be willing to explore it before judging it.

What language should you speak?

Himid’s paintings are about communication, but she uses a visual language that many of us don’t know well. She speaks through colour, brushstrokes, gesture, and emotion. Even with my years in the arts, I found them hard to interpret at first.

There’s a difference between not understanding an idea and it not communicating at all. I was getting something from the paintings before I could put it into words. The colour and energy had already made an impression on me, even if I hadn’t fully understood them yet.

Over time, I realized that one painting was about boat building, another about architects, and so on. The more time I spent with the paintings, the more I noticed, because I stopped looking for an instant answer.

Not long ago, I did some freelance work with a tech company where the marketing creatives and engineers struggled to agree on how to talk to their audience. The creatives wanted to connect through feelings and experiences, while the engineers focused on logic and data. This kind of gap is common, and many of my freelance workshops help bridge it.

Neither side was wrong. One group focused on what people needed to know, and the other on what people needed to feel. My exercises helped them learn to connect with their audience’s emotions and logic.

Communication is more than just sending information that people understand right away. Ideas, like Himid’s, can come through atmosphere, feeling, or experience before their meaning is clear.

The Lesson for Work and Life

These communication skills matter even more in business than in art, such as when an entrepreneur faces a situation with no clear answers, like when new technology appears or a surprise opportunity comes up. If you can handle uncertainty without rushing to a quick fix, you have an advantage. We often lose our best ideas by judging them too soon, before they have a chance to grow.

It’s much harder, but much better, to ask questions than to judge. If, instead of looking at a painting or a business problem and asking, “What does this mean?” we ask, “What’s interesting about this?” or “Where could this take us?” we will find ourselves in a more fruitful place. The most successful entrepreneurs and creative thinkers aren’t the ones searching for a specific answer, but the ones asking interesting questions. Innovation happens in the space between confusion and understanding.

Looking at art helps you get used to not knowing all the answers. Himid’s paintings taught me that I don’t have to understand everything right away. At first, I wanted to work them out, but then I started to just experience them. The more time I spent with them, the more I noticed. The more I tried to appreciate her ideas instead of explaining them right away, the more rewarding it was. New ideas often work the same way. At first, they can seem odd or even unsettling.

When we come across something confusing—whether it’s a piece of art, a new strategy at work, or a new idea—we shouldn’t rush to understand it. Give it some time. What confuses us most at first often ends up changing how we think.

item.title: Creativizing the Self
item.description:
Creativity

Creativizing the Self

Why we don’t simply discover who we are. We create who we become.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Meaning can follow action. We don’t always need to know why before we begin.
  • Making is a form of discovery. Creative action can reveal what matters to us.
  • Creativity reshapes identity. What we create can change how we understand ourselves.
  • Uncertainty can be productive. Sometimes clarity only becomes possible after we act.
Surreal fragmented faces representing the complex nature of human consciousness and identity
Source: Adinuranjaya Adobe Stock

The Trap of Finding Yourself

We spend years trying to discover who we are—everything from astrology to therapy. We collect labels that we identify with: extrovert, artistic, spiritual, and more. These labels may contain some truth about our temperament, history, and what we take to be our experience, but when our description becomes our destiny, we may find danger. Our identity becomes our constraint.

Over 30 years ago, I coined the term creativizing from observing people who added creativity to everyday activities. I felt we needed a more active term to describe the dynamic act of creating as applied to the most ordinary activity: washing the dishes, walking the dog, writing a note to an old friend. It’s more than just adaptation. It’s the active engagement with the circumstances at hand. A disappointment can become a new direction. An unexpected interest could become a new pursuit. An old, worn-out belief could be a new possibility.

Over the years, the idea evolved. I began to see how the process of creativizing not only brought new ideas and pathways into the world, but also changed the people who were creativizing— the things we create create us. The implication is a completely different understanding of our identity. We don’t discover it. We create it.

The Self Is Raw Material

“Finding yourself,” that Summer of Love chestnut, assumes an authentic self is buried underneath all your obligations, expectations, and wrong turns. The finished self awaits to be sprung like Michelangelo carving David from a block of marble. But that view denies agency. We are ever active participants in our becoming. This does not mean we have unlimited capability to self-invent, or be anything we want. We have inherited the raw material of the self: family, culture, natural abilities, limitations, opportunities, and outrageous fortune. Surely, our experiences, relationships, roles, and personal narrative shape identity. Behavior is, in fact, evidence of our identity, for our actions demonstrate changes in our self-perception. But the old question, “Who am I really?” often overshadows and even subjugates the newer one: “What might I become?”

Self-confirming identity leads us on a search for confirming evidence. The simple question “Who am I?” may become a barrier to creativizing the self. This approach searches for confirming feedback and discounts contradictions. Creativizing reopens identity. Not the wholesale reinvention that we so often seek, but rather, permission to remain unfinished.

Act Before You Become

Identity can be a trap. We often wait for internal changes in anticipation of external actions. For example, we may believe that more discipline will lead to better food choices and regular exercise. But how does this actually happen? The conventional sequence: “Who am I?” “What do I do?” In essence, it’s cause and effect. The creativizing sequence is “What do I actually do? What am I experiencing? Who am I becoming?” It’s a core reversal. Behavior is not always a consequence of identity. Often, identity is a consequence of behavior. For example, most accomplished writers will tell you that writing badly precedes becoming a writer. Dale Carnegie, one of the original self-help gurus, understood this well when he encouraged his program participants to speak even when afraid. It wasn’t just to improve their speaking prowess, but, more importantly, to develop their courage. Experience doesn’t just reveal character; it creates it.

No Dramatic Reinvention Is Required

You don’t have to quit your job, lose your spouse, or move to Bali. Creativizing is done in small experiments. Want to change your life? Start by driving to work a different way. Say hi to someone you haven’t talked to before. Sign up for a class to develop a new skill. No declarations of complete transformation required. All that is needed are small opportunities for another self to emerge. This does not require excessive optimism, aphorisms, or over-devotion to positive thinking.

Creativizing is distinct from conventional self-improvement in that it doesn’t assume a predetermined ideal—the gap between the current self and the ideal self. In this view, the improvement is an effort to close the gap. However, when creativizing, there is no finished destination. You enter the experience to discover what the experience calls forth. The possible outcomes range from failure to an unexpected realization. “I didn’t know I could do that.” What you are doing is moving the boundary of the self. It is through experimentation and experience that we learn what is possible. Our identity is born out of our everyday practices. This, of course, creates the fundamental paradox of this point of view. You don’t become different before living differently. By living differently, you become different. This means we must pay attention, not merely to what we create, but to how what we create re-creates us. This makes the self our greatest work of art.

Everything You Create Creates You

In the conventional one-way self-help model, the gardener creates the garden, the writer creates the story, and the parent creates the child. Now think of it the other way around. The garden creates patience in the gardener. The story creates insight in the writer. The child creates the parent's ability to nurture. Everything you create creates you. Conventionally, we measure creation as an outcome. Did it succeed? Did the relationship last? Did I accomplish the goal? What we overlook is another question: Who did I become by doing it? Both success and failure are formative. How we mitigate the risk and reward of trying something new is by doing smaller things differently. They are tells. They show what is emerging.

The world is unfinished, and so are we. This is not a deficiency. This is not a problem requiring a solution. This is a possibility. Maybe we’ve been asking the wrong questions all along: Who am I? Who do I want to be? Instead, perhaps we should focus more on the infinite movements of transformation opposed to the finite beginning and end states. What if there is no there? What if the whole point of the journey is how it changes us? Creativizing, doing small things in creative ways, may be the very destination we seek.

item.title: Are We Raising Bonsai Trees or Wildflowers?
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Are We Raising Bonsai Trees or Wildflowers?

Personal Perspective: When a child's ambition challenges your philosophy.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Our greatest gift to our children may be the courage, gratitude, and compassion to choose their own path.
  • Protecting children from uncertainty may leave them less prepared to navigate the world they'll inherit.
  • Our children need more than opportunities to succeed. They need the wisdom to decide what's worth pursuing.
  • Sometimes the greatest act of parental love is knowing when to put down the pencil and let children draw.

It was Sunday, and I had already spent the morning speaking with a refugee family facing an asylum hearing before a newly appointed former ICE attorney. According to what records we could find, the attorney had not granted asylum to anyone before him. The family had limited savings and no safe choice; they had to decide whether to spend what little they had on a lawyer to fight for the life they’d built here, or preserve that money for the possibility of beginning somewhere else. The conversation weighed on me all day, its impossible arithmetic lodged somewhere between my ribs.

A few hours later, I was sitting down for a mother-daughter high tea at the Drake Hotel in Chicago, and the transition felt almost obscene with silver teapots and delicate china, tiered trays crowded with tiny sandwiches and immaculate pastries, chandeliers glowing overhead, and all the lovely excess of a room designed to make abundance feel effortless. After the morning I'd just spent contemplating how much hope a family could afford to gamble, I felt as though I'd wandered through some invisible door and landed at a Capitol feast from The Hunger Games. And then, surrounded by all that affluence, we began talking about what every parent eventually talks about: Our children.

Did I Miss the Memo?

My daughter is 15, a sophomore in an extraordinarily rigorous academic program, and apparently, I'd missed a memo. Everyone was touring colleges. Not seniors or even juniors. Sophomores. One person at the table had toured as a freshman.

There was summer school, too, not because anyone was struggling, but apparently they had another rung to climb. Kids took extra courses over the summer so they could move into more advanced math the following year, which would presumably position them for the next class, and then the one after that. Summers had plans, and the plans had plans. There I was, halfway through a tiny cucumber sandwich (so good, by the way), realizing that I was a few moves behind.

I guess I should be used to this by now. I've been living among tiger parents since my children were small, and I know the familiar choreography of parental comparison. Someone's 5-year-old is reading at a seventh-grade level. Someone else's 8-year-old has a private fencing coach. By middle school, another child has somehow founded a nonprofit between soccer practice and dinner. It's easy to think: Wait. Am I supposed to be doing this? After enough years of this, though, I'd learned to catch myself, realign, and smile appreciatively without immediately recalculating my own kids' futures.

Aye, simple. I'd once heard a metaphor on a parenting podcast that stuck: Are we raising bonsai trees or wildflowers? A bonsai is cultivated with extraordinary devotion—watered and protected, studied and tended, but it is also continually trimmed and shaped. But no one stands over a wildflower deciding which direction every stem should take or trimming it each time it grows beyond the boundaries of someone else's imagined design. The gulf between our conversations that day was almost grotesque, and I wondered how to take my daughter's worries seriously without losing sight of what I'd witnessed that morning.

The Transition from Architect to Supporter

I looked at my daughter's face and recognized the dawning suspicion that her mother might not have been properly preparing her for the future she'd already begun designing for herself. That look changed things, because she isn't 5 anymore. Back then, I chose the school, the activities, the bedtime, and whether another cookie was a good idea. I drew most of the boundaries of her little world, and she grew inside them. For better or worse, I was the architect. Now, at 15, brilliant and ambitious, she has plans; ambitions I didn't plant, and ideas about what she wants that sometimes arrive fully formed before I've had a chance to decide what I think.

I’ve now moved beyond how much I should shape my child's future because I’m parenting someone who’s begun trying to form it for herself. And she's great at adding lines I hadn't imagined and erasing some I thought were permanent. I have to figure out when to offer a hand, when to question what she’s drawing, and when to have the humility to put the pencil down and let the picture become hers. The distinction between cultivation and control crumbled before my eyes, and refusing to optimize my daughter began to look, at least to the not-so-young-person herself, remarkably like failing to support her. We tend to talk about achievement pressure as though it travels neatly in one direction: adults impose it, children absorb it; parents push, children either perform or buckle beneath the weight. Ooph. By adolescence, the current runs both ways! Our children are no longer growing inside the worlds we create for them. They look beyond us, absorbing the ambitions and anxieties of their peers, schools, and culture, and deciding which of those ambitions they want to claim as their own.

The stakes of the two conversations I had that day were, of course, nowhere near equivalent. And yet, can I judge my daughter's concerns by the standards of my adult mind, the one that had spent the morning with refugees and hope gambling? I honestly do not know. My task wasn't really to answer that, but something far more convoluted. I had to decide when to protect her from the undue pressure around her, when to show her the ugliness of the real world, and to get out of her way and let her forge her path.

One of parenting's deepest seductions is the belief that enough vigilance can become certainty. If I choose the right school and the right classes, expose my children to enough of the world while protecting them from its sharpest edges, recognize exactly when to push and exactly when to pull back, I can arrange the pieces carefully enough that their lives will unfold toward safety, happiness, wisdom, and success. Of course, it's an illusion. I can't give her a life without uncertainty, and I'm beginning to suspect that trying to do so might leave her less prepared for the one she'll actually have. No philosophy, ancient or modern, can make those decisions for me. Stoicism does, however, help me move beyond asking whether I should optimize my daughter for the future, toward something far more important: Who does she need to become so that she can choose well when I'm no longer there to choose with her?

Instilling a Resilient Future

I want her to have the courage to pursue something difficult without believing that courage requires her to pursue it forever. I want her to know how to work extraordinarily hard without confusing exhaustion with virtue, and to have the wisdom to recognize when working harder is no longer the answer, sit down, and take a rest. I want her to feel disappointed, but I don't want her to mistake that pain for evidence that she has failed at life. I want her to be ambitious without becoming captive to ambition, and confident enough in her own judgment. Kids should question the status quo and choose their path, even when conforming with the momentum around her is easier.

Boy, I’d love for her to run like hell.

Maybe we’ll tour colleges this year, but either way, being “behind” is only terrifying when you’ve accepted someone else's definition of ahead. I keep coming back to the wildflower. My job was never to choose between carefully cultivating her and letting her grow on her own. She needs roots and tending, but I need to know when to hand her the shears. Her life is increasingly her own; whether I shaped her this way or that doesn't really matter. When the shaping is finally hers, she will know what to nurture, what to cut away, and what to let grow wild, with the courage to do all three.

And somewhere in the distance between that family's impossible morning and my daughter's hopeful afternoon, I found the only promise I could reasonably make her: I would do my best to help her become wise enough to navigate a world neither of us could control, grateful enough to recognize the extraordinary gifts of her own life, and compassionate enough to understand that for others, the choices that shape a future have nothing to do with getting ahead, and everything to do with finding a way to begin again.

item.title: Stop Waiting for Perfection Before You Praise Your Child
item.description:
Parenting

Stop Waiting for Perfection Before You Praise Your Child

How to use praise to strengthen the behaviors you want to see more often.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Don’t wait for the behavior you ultimately want; reinforce the pieces of it as they begin to appear.
  • Work backward from your end goal. Identify and praise the smaller steps that will move your child toward it.
  • Corrective feedback can feel like criticism when children hear little about what they’re doing well.
  • Raise the bar as your child succeeds and praise progress along the way.

Some parents and even teachers today struggle with when and what to praise. They believe that children should do what they are told or asked to do simply because it is expected of them. Others are reluctant to praise behaviors that fall short of the end behavior they expect. Many parents think of praise as something that comes after an achievement. They worry that praise of this sort will create dependence, reduce motivation, or make their child expect recognition for every task they engage in, much less accomplish. Some parents wonder, as their child ages, whether they will aspire to anything that is remotely effortful.

But praise can serve another, more important purpose. Rather than simply recognizing a behavior after it has been mastered, praise can help increase the behaviors that eventually lead to the desired end goal. This is why waiting until your child fully meets an expectation before offering praise can be a mistake, or at least slow progress toward the intended goal. A child may need praise most while they are still learning and trying to master a new skill.

Source: SDI Productions / Getty Images Signature

During this process of acquiring a new skill, you may be withholding praise or approval or offering corrective feedback, hoping to encourage your child to work harder or help them improve. But if your child is already receiving a great deal of corrective feedback, withholding encouragement may simply leave them hearing much more about what they are doing wrong than what they are doing right. What you intend as motivating feedback is often instead experienced by your child as criticism. Over time, they may become increasingly resistant to the very feedback intended to help them.

Interestingly, researchers who have studied happy and stable adult relationships have found that positive interactions substantially outweigh negative ones. John Gottman’s research found a ratio of about five positive interactions for every one negative interaction. It is probably not surprising that many who work with children, who may be more sensitive to corrective feedback than adults, suggest aiming for an even stronger ratio of positives to negatives. Peg Dawson, a psychologist whose work has focused on children with ADHD and, more specifically, executive function challenges, has recommended about 10 instances of praise for every one correction.

Don’t Wait for the Perfect Outcome

Behavior does not need to be perfect to warrant recognition. If you don’t yet see the end-goal behavior, praise the behaviors that would naturally come before it. I often ask teachers to think about where they would place a child in terms of the behaviors they are seeing. If it seems that they are behaving like a child two years younger, then what would they expect of that child? A more scaffolded approach adjusts your expectations to the developmental level at which your child is functioning.

Source: Fizke / Getty Images Signature

Give the benefit of the doubt and assume that it is rare that a child is deliberately antagonizing you as a parent; most children are not setting out to disappoint, frustrate, or annoy you. Rather than assume or be disappointed in what your child should already be doing, ask yourself, “What is reasonable given where my child currently is?” The question then becomes, “What can I notice and reinforce that will help them move closer to the behavior I want to see?”

For a child, parental praise is one of the strongest rewards. Praise is also a form of positive attention, and most children will do a lot for attention. Although positive attention may be more desirable than negative attention, children may engage in behaviors that result in either. Oftentimes, adults inadvertently give more attention, through criticism or correction, to a child’s falling short of the goal than to praising an approximation of the goal.

Because attention can be especially reinforcing for children, even when it is negative or corrective, the corrective attention you give your child with the goal of decreasing or stopping a particular behavior may actually increase it. We may also expect that, with minimal practice and no steps in between, a child will engage in the end goal behavior. But that expectation is probably unreasonable. Instead, a baby step in the desired direction can be praised and then followed with a slight increase in what the child needs to do in order to learn the reward or praise.

Whenever giving praise, it should be intentional and specific, letting the child know exactly what they did that you liked and reinforcing the behaviors that are moving your child toward the goal, even when they are not there yet. The praise should help the child understand what behavior you want to see more often.

Think about a behavior you would like your child to develop. Perhaps you want your six-year-old to stop interrupting conversations, clean up independently, get dressed without repeated reminders, or handle disappointment without becoming upset. The end goal may seem very far from what your child is doing today. Rather than waiting until your child can demonstrate the finished behavior, identify the smaller steps that would naturally come before it. One way to do this is to think about the behavior you hope to see six months or a year from now. Then work backward. What smaller steps would move your child in that direction?

Praise those efforts, and then coach your child privately toward the next step. If you need to offer guidance in public, do so in a manner that does not call attention to their deficit relative to expectations or peers. One of the worst experiences is to be shamed, and being shamed publicly is worse still.

Praise the Steps That Lead to the Goal

Imagine a six-year-old who frequently interrupts conversations. The end goal might be waiting patiently until others are finished speaking. Rather than waiting to praise only perfect self-control, you might say, “I noticed you waited for me to say a few sentences before telling me what you wanted to say. That was helpful.” Later, you might privately encourage them to try waiting even longer next time. As your child becomes more successful, you can gradually raise your expectations.

Source: blackCAT / Getty Images Signature

Be Intentional About What You Notice

For children who struggle with behavior, it can be helpful to have a plan. Rather than trying to notice everything, identify one or two specific behaviors you would like to increase. Then look for opportunities to acknowledge those behaviors when they occur.

At the same time, we don’t want to inadvertently reinforce behavior we don’t want to see. When possible, irrelevant behavior can be ignored, and attention can be focused on the behaviors we want to encourage.

Praise Along the Way, Not Just When They Get There

Nobody waits until a kicker can make a 50-yard field goal before acknowledging progress. You start closer, reinforce success, and gradually increase the distance. The same principle applies when you are trying to shape a child’s behavior. Praise the approximation of the end goal, then gradually increase what you expect before the praise or reward is given.

Don’t think of praise as a reward for perfection, but as a shaping tool that can help move your child closer and closer to the desired end-goal behavior. Don’t wait until your child has reached the goal to acknowledge their progress. Praise along the way can help them get there.
