item.title: Letting Your Stories Be Co-Authored
item.description:
Identity

Letting Your Stories Be Co-Authored

Your story doesn’t develop in isolation. Choose the right kind of editors.

Posted October 9, 2026

Imagine you quit your job. It was the kind of corporate job you dreamed of getting as a college freshman, complete with cushy benefits and upward mobility. But your mental health plummeted a month into the work. You felt yourself becoming someone you didn’t recognize. Last week, you decided enough was enough – and you left.

Today, you tell your family about it. Your mom says that this is who you’ve always been: a quitter. When you didn’t like piano lessons at age 5, you quit. When you turned out to be a terrible trombone player at age 11, you quit. But your dad says something different: You’ve always known your own mind. When the most popular kid in school asked you to the homecoming dance at age 15, you decided to go with your friends instead. When all your friends wanted to go to Cancun for spring break at age 19, you decided to join your parents in Ireland.

These are two very different storylines. Both have the opportunity to be integrated into your emerging story about this career transition. And most people don’t realize that such co-authored narratives have seeped beneath the surface until the story about who they are is already entrenched: I’m a quitter.

The Listeners Who Shape Us

We tend to think of memory as a private archive. But psychologist Monisha Pasupathi has shown that remembering is a social act: The way we talk about our past with others shapes what we remember and how we understand it (Pasupathi, 2001). Each time you tell a story about yourself, your listener’s reactions help decide which details remain, what the experience means, and what it says about who you are. Over time, these small everyday tellings build into a larger sense of self (McLean, Pasupathi, & Pals, 2007).

Listeners matter even when they say very little. In one set of studies, people told friends about a recent experience. When friends were distracted, speakers had a harder time holding onto their own view of themselves. Surprisingly, friends who openly disagreed didn’t have the same effect (Pasupathi & Rich, 2005). Responsiveness, more than agreement, seemed to keep people anchored in their own self-understanding. Other research found that young adults told more meaningful, interpretive stories about their experiences when talking with responsive friends (Pasupathi & Hoyt, 2009).

This means your mom’s “quitter” story doesn’t need to win an argument to become ingrained. It only needs to be repeated at enough holiday dinners.

When Loved Ones Hold the Pen

Close relationships don’t just shape how we tell our stories; they shape who we become. Researchers call this the Michelangelo phenomenon: when a partner sees us in ways that match our ideal self and treats us accordingly, we tend to grow toward that ideal (Drigotas et al., 1999). Like a sculptor revealing a figure hidden in stone, a loving partner can help bring out the person we’re trying to become. Or a loving father can remind you that you’ve always known who you want to become.

But the process can work in reverse, too: A loved one who consistently sees us through a smaller lens can chip us into a shape that doesn’t fit.

Choosing Your Editors

You can’t write your story alone, nor should you want to. But you can decide which voices get editing privileges.

  • Notice whose voice you’re hearing. When a familiar verdict about yourself surfaces, like “I always give up,” ask yourself where you first heard it. Tracing it to a specific person gives you the chance to evaluate it rather than simply absorb it.
  • Test the storyline against your values. The same life events supported both the quitter story and the knows-her-own-mind story. Choosing between them is about authorship. You’re allowed to choose the one that reflects what you care about.
  • Keep the note, drop the label. Even unkind editors sometimes carry useful feedback. Your mom’s comment might prompt a fair question: Do I leave things when they get hard, or when they stop fitting? You can keep the question without adopting the label.
  • Bring tender stories to responsive listeners first. When a chapter is still in draft mode, share it with people who ask questions rather than deliver verdicts. Their attention helps you discover what the story means to you before others attempt to decide it for you.

Your loved ones will always have a hand in your story but there are ways to make sure you remain the one deciding what makes the final cut.

item.title: Choosing Leaders With Dark Personalities
item.description:
Personality

Choosing Leaders With Dark Personalities

Those with dark personalities can often be seductive and difficult to weed out.

Posted October 9, 2026

Dark personalities—narcissism, psychopathy and Machiavellianism—are collectively referred to as the Dark Triad. What they have in common is “a tendency to callously use others for personal gain.”1 But their differences are significant. Machiavellians know what they want and can be patient long-term awaiting their goals. Narcissists need ego stroking and validation and are drawn to the spotlight. Narcissists minimize others and blame others when their own decision-making goes wrong. Psychopaths, on the other hand, are impulsive and thrill-seeking, live in the moment, pay no attention to rules, and would throw away their whole life for the right kind of excitement.2

Source: Olcay Ertem/Pixabay

Dark traits more evident in men

According to psychologists Dr. Craig Neumann and Dr. Barry Kaufman, dark personalities come in different “shades” and degrees, and “approximately 1-2 percent of individuals in the general population display extremely dark personality features,” while 10-20 percent of individuals have moderately elevated levels. Their analysis concluded that “These traits are far more evident, on average, in men than women.” 3

The allure of those with dark traits

For the most part, many people are attracted to these personality types because they have an aura of self-confidence and strength that can appear engaging. This is especially true when it serves their needs. Some may appear to have strong leadership abilities and “in corporate settings, those with dark personality traits are slightly more likely to emerge as leaders and are seen as charismatic.”4 But they can also draw a dichotomy of opinions -- some are captivated by them, others are repelled.

Are these people the successful leaders that they appear to be?

According to Neumann and Kaufman, “their success in the real world is questionable.”5 They can seem to be great negotiators, but they generally fail to work cooperatively in a team effort. Instead, their approach would be self-serving, seeking to maximize their personal gain.

Sometimes these people can gain powerful positions in the corporate world, law and politics. In fact, research shows that “political figures with dark personality traits are more likely to get elected to public office and remain there, though studies show that they are much poorer at getting legislation passed.”6

Often, these people aspire to be iconic, sounding bold and convincing. They may take credit for other people’s work and use others to do their work. “Overall, individuals with dark traits engage in more counterproductive work behaviors, such as theft and abusive supervision.” 7

Positive leaders vs. those with dark personalities

But what about people who are “positive”— those who are genuinely interested in doing a good job? Research conducted by Timothy Judge, a management professor at the University of Notre Dame, has shown that agreeable people -- those who are cooperative, nice and gentle -- are less likely to emerge as leaders.”8 However, working with someone with a dark personality can wreak havoc with an organization and ruin people’s reputations and careers.

On the one hand, we want people whom we can trust, but somehow, we are duped by the polished speaker who comes on like the proverbial “house on fire” and is willing to take big risks. According to Dr. Bill Wales, professor of management at James Madison University in Harrisonburg, VA, bad bosses “are more likely to take big risks or make bold moves, which may end up being major coups or miserable failures.”9

So how do we tell who will be a gifted leader? The answer is elusive, but paying very close attention to the real accomplishments of others may be a good starting point. According to Dr. Paul Babiak, industrial organizational psychologist, we need “better vetting procedures. Even so, it is likely that sour cream will continue to rise to the top.”10

item.title: Embedding Lived Experience in the Heart of CBT Practice
item.description:
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

Embedding Lived Experience in the Heart of CBT Practice

What those who have experienced therapy can teach those who deliver it.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Lived experience voices can improve development, delivery and governance of psychological therapies.
  • For lived experience to make real difference, it takes meaningful engagement, not one-off consultations.
  • Clinicians with personal experience of distress, stigma and support have powerful expertise.
  • Practitioners who want to draw on their own lived experience need good practice guides to do so appropriately.

The value of lived experience in shaping mental health practice has never been clearer.

The voices of those with personal experience of mental health challenges and cognitive behavioural therapy—services users, carers, the public and practitioners—have to be meaningfully heard if they are to improve how psychological therapies are developed, delivered and governed.

Lived experience should not be optional or an afterthought. It has an important role in good practice, strong professional standards and public trust. CBT is at its best when it is informed not only by research evidence and clinical expertise, but also by the real experiences of the people it is designed to support.

Those voices add to the body of knowledge supporting it and can be used to help build the structures, culture and opportunities that place lived experience alongside professional expertise, so clinicians can practice with both excellence and humanity.

Embedding public lived experience in decisions

Those who receive CBT can offer professional bodies, clinicians and healthcare organisations valuable insights that cannot be gained through professional training alone. Everyone who experiences therapy does so through the lens of their intersectional identities and lived experience.

Those insights can enrich clinicians’ understanding of what good care feels like in practice, highlight the barriers to effective therapy and help identify ways to make services safer as well as more inclusive.

Achieving this means moving beyond one-off consultations towards meaningful engagement with lived experience networks, involving them in policy and training committees or advising on specific projects.

Done meaningfully, this will not only help create better practice, but generate and maintain public trust.

The value of dual expertise

Many clinicians hold dual expertise: their professional knowledge as practitioners, supervisors, trainers or researchers, alongside their own lived experience of mental health difficulties.

These perspectives help bridge the gap between theory and reality. This powerful and often under-recognised form of expertise combines the technical understanding of CBT with personal insight into what it means to navigate distress, stigma and support.

Providing opportunities for this dual expertise to be heard is important to challenge the commonly held idea that professional and lived identities should be kept separate while recognising the need for appropriate professional and therapeutic boundaries.

This does not mean practitioners should routinely discuss their personal experiences with clients. Decisions about self-disclosure require careful professional judgement. But practitioners' lived experience can provide valuable insights into how care is developed and delivered. This will benefit the people they work with.

Lived experience and public protection

At first glance, lived experience and quality assurance may seem like separate agendas. However, take a second look and you’ll see that they are deeply connected. The safest and highest-quality care is care that is responsive to the needs, values and realities of the people receiving it.

Embedding lived experience into accreditation, standards, policy and complaints procedures strengthens accountability. Public trust will grow when people can see that decisions are informed by those directly affected. Their experiences help practitioners and organisations ask better questions, notice blind spots sooner and continuously improve our understanding of what high-quality CBT should look like.

Embedding public voices and platforming dual expertise of members while strengthening quality and public protection are connected by a simple principle: The best CBT comes out of a collaboration of evidence, professional knowledge and lived experience. Lasting change will come through modifying how we listen, lead and make decisions. That means building meaningful partnerships, challenging tokenism and ensuring lived experience has real influence.

Lived experience can complement and deepen clinical excellence by helping define, measure and sustain it. In doing so, organisations and individual practitioners can continue to protect the public, support their members and promote a therapy that is not only evidence-based, but truly person-centered.

Creating lived experience networks within professional bodies is an effective step towards this. So is publishing good practice guides for practitioners who want to draw on their lived experience appropriately.

Success will come not simply from inviting the voice of lived experience into the room but ensuring that happens early enough and is taken seriously enough to influence the decisions being made.

Tanya Marwaha
Source: Tanya Marwaha

Tanya Marwaha is Lived Experience Lead for the British Association for Behavioural and Cognitive Psychotherapies. She is a multi-award winning mental health, suicide and disability speaker and cultural competency educator.

item.title: 2 Ways to Kill the "Sunday Evening Blues"
item.description:
Happiness

2 Ways to Kill the "Sunday Evening Blues"

Here's how to avoid the shadow that looms over you every Sunday evening.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Many of us struggle with the reality check that Sunday evenings tend to be.
  • Social connection and engagement in leisure activities with others can transform mental health and well-being.
  • Sleep consistency and adequate sleep duration are essential for mood enhancement and anxiety reduction.
Source: Amir Selfish / Pexels

Sunday evenings are a notoriously difficult time for many of us. Whether it’s the sinking feeling from realizing another weekend has passed while you were idly scrolling through TikTok, or discovering the pile of work you intended to catch up on over the weekend, many of us struggle with the reality check that Sunday evenings tend to bring.

However, there are a few science-backed strategies you can use to recalibrate your mind to make the last hours of the weekend exciting rather than anxiety-inducing. Here are two.

1. Engage in Shared Activities With People You Connect With to Keep the Sunday Blues at Bay

Research has shown that social connection and engagement in leisure activities with others can have a transformative impact on mental health and well-being.

For instance, a 2020 study found that among factors associated with depression, including lack of sleep, weak social connection, and an unhealthy diet, a strong and robust social circle was the strongest protective factor for depression. This was true even in the case of individuals who may have had a genetic or biological predisposition toward depressive symptoms.

Another 2020 study conducted at Harvard University and published in the Journal of Positive Psychology and Wellbeing found that when it comes to shared activities, picking activities that have to do with your social relationships and institutional commitments, like volunteering for a cause you care about or joining a community organization, can have a substantial effect on well-being.

By engaging in shared activities with people you connect with, you can strengthen your social connections and improve your mood. This can help reduce anxiety and feelings of loneliness, which are common on Sunday evenings. Whether it’s going for a walk with a friend, organizing a pickleball tournament in your neighborhood, or participating in a group fitness class, there are many ways to engage in shared activities with others.

Making time for these activities on Sunday evenings not only improves your mood and reduces anxiety but also makes the final hours of your weekend more enjoyable. Plus, as an added bonus, if you have something fun to look forward to on a Sunday evening, you’d have no time to wallow in your Sunday sadness.

2. Maintain a Consistent Sleep-Wake Cycle

A 2021 study assessed sleep with a wearable device, daily mood with a smartphone application, and depression with a nine-item Patient Health Questionnaire among 2,115 trainee physicians over the demanding first year of physician training. It found that reduced total sleep time and later bedtime, along with increased variability in total sleep time and in wake time, were associated with more depressive symptoms in the long term. In the short term, the study found that the absence of a consistent circadian rhythm led to poorer mood throughout the following day.

Thus, maintaining sleep consistency and ensuring adequate sleep duration are essential for mood enhancement and anxiety reduction, especially if you find that your sleep patterns shift drastically over the weekends.

To reclaim your Sunday evenings, one of the best things you can do is set a regular bedtime and stick to it, even on weekends. This can help your body clock adjust to a consistent rhythm and make it easier to fall asleep and wake up at the same time every day. Another way is to expose yourself to natural light in the morning, which can help signal to your brain that it is time to wake up and start the day. You can also use an alarm clock that gradually increases brightness or volume, or plays pleasant sounds or music, to make waking up gentler and more enjoyable.

Leveraging the benefits of social interactions and maintaining a consistent sleep cycle are proven methods to elevate your mood. Implementing these approaches not only provides immediate relief to your Sunday evening blues but also shifts your perception of weekends as a whole. Instead of dreading the last hours of your weekend, you’ll have the tools to make them a highlight, ensuring that every bit of your weekend is enjoyed to its fullest.

item.title: How Psychodynamic Therapy Can Change Problematic Behavior
item.description:
Therapy

How Psychodynamic Therapy Can Change Problematic Behavior

Identifying psychodynamic contributors and developing strategies for change.

Posted October 9, 2026

Key points
  • Problematic behaviors may persist because they protect self-esteem and manage painful feelings and conflicts.
  • Understanding dynamic contributors to problematic behaviors can help patients develop more adaptive responses.
  • Transference and countertransference can create obstacles to behavioral change that need to be addressed.
  • Trying new behaviors can reveal unrecognized expectations and conflicts, facilitating insight and change.
Source: inspiringteam/Shutterstock

People often recognize that certain behaviors, or avoidance of certain actions, are causing difficulties, yet still find themselves repeating the behaviors. They may be aware that they drink too much, repeatedly lose their temper, take on more responsibility than they can manage, or avoid confronting an unfair boss. Understanding the sources of these behaviors is useful, but insight by itself does not necessarily lead to change.

Psychoanalytic approaches have traditionally eschewed targeting behavioral changes, believing that such efforts do not address the core issues that contribute to problems. Problem-focused psychodynamic psychotherapy (PrFPP) (Busch, 2022) works to identify specific problems, explore the psychological factors that contribute to them, and help patients develop more adaptive ways of responding to their relationships and environment. Such efforts include identifying the context and emotions, early experiences, representations of self and others, and intrapsychic conflicts to address and change problematic inhibitions and behaviors (Busch, 2018; Busch, 2025).

Identifying Problematic Inhibitions or Behaviors

PrFPP identifies behaviors as problematic when they cause recurrent difficulties for the patient and the patient seems unable to shift or change them. Patients may describe certain behaviors as problematic, but they may not recognize others (such as drinking or overwork), sometimes due to painful feelings or internal conflicts these behaviors manage. PrFPP can be useful in helping patients acknowledge and address these problems.

Identifying and Addressing Factors That Make Behavior Difficult to Change

Several factors can contribute to persistent problematic behaviors. These inhibitions or actions may, for example, temporarily reduce anxiety, protect self-esteem, diminish intrapsychic and interpersonal conflict, express anger indirectly, or avoid painful feelings. An individual who chronically agrees to unreasonable requests, for example, may want to become more assertive but experience guilt when considering such a response, or anticipate criticism and/or rejection.

Using PrFPP, the therapist addresses factors that interfere with changing these behaviors (Busch, 2018; Busch, 2022). Therapist and patient work to understand what triggers the inhibition or behavior, what feelings accompany it, what is accomplished emotionally, and what the patient fears might happen if it changed. A psychodynamic framework for behavioral change includes identifying and addressing a series of contributors: the situations and emotions surrounding the behavior; childhood experiences that helped shape it; recurring negative expectations of oneself and others; conflicts and coping strategies that make change difficult; and limitations in understanding one's own or other people's motives. The therapist and patient identify alternative behaviors and examine the feelings and expectations that arise when the patient imagines trying or actually attempts them.

Transference and Countertransference Factors

Psychodynamic approaches add another layer of value in accomplishing behavioral change by considering transference and countertransference factors that can interfere with such efforts. For example, patients may rebel against efforts to help them shift behaviors, experiencing the therapist as an authority attempting to compel change, despite having consciously agreed to such efforts. Additionally, the patient can feel guilty or fearful about such changes, creating resistance to the therapy. The therapist works to identify and ease such conflicts. Patients may also wish to please therapists by making changes, leading to guilt or feelings of being a “bad patient” when they have difficulty accomplishing them. Finally, the patient can become dependent on the therapist, requesting recurrent help with decision making rather than pursuing autonomy.

Therapists should also be alert to countertransference factors that might disrupt efforts at behavioral change. For example, therapists might develop a sense of certainty about how patients should behave. The therapist may believe he has better judgment than the patient regarding particular actions, but he should consider that he is only hearing the patient’s perspective and focus on developing the patient’s autonomy. For instance, a patient may report that her boss is behaving in a hostile or judgmental manner when in reality the boss is appropriately pressing the patient to complete essential tasks. Suggesting that the patient confront her boss or leave her job may reinforce problematic patterns without adequately addressing her underlying narcissistic sensitivity. Therapists should also be aware of frustration or disappointment about a patient’s difficulty changing. Such attitudes may be inadvertently communicated to the patient, potentially triggering feelings of inadequacy or of being a “bad patient.” Additionally, therapists should be alert to getting into power struggles, pressing patients to make changes or overriding patients’ concerns about suggested behaviors.

A Collaborative Approach to Behavioral Change

This approach reduces the risk of conflicts between therapist and patient regarding behavioral change by highlighting collaborative aspects of the process (Busch, 2018). They work together in identifying problems and their contributors. When considering alternative behaviors, the therapist can discuss how they cannot be certain of the best action in a given situation and some experimentation will be needed. Therapists can encourage patients to raise concerns about behavioral suggestions.

Experimenting with New Behaviors

Considering and trying new behaviors is useful in finding more adaptive ways of coping. For example, the therapist can discuss with the patient ways in which she might express her feelings directly when such a possibility frightens her. She can imagine what she anticipates the other person’s response will be. If the patient has difficulty trying these behaviors, these efforts help identify the psychological obstacles to change. A patient who plans to ask for a raise may suddenly feel ashamed, greedy, frightened, or convinced that the boss will become hostile. Those reactions provide important information about the meanings attached to assertiveness.

Homework, a nonstandard approach for psychodynamic psychotherapy, can also be valuable. Patients may use a diary to keep track of situations that trigger behaviors, note what they were feeling just beforehand, or delay an impulsive action long enough to observe what is driving it. Such strategies are often found to increase psychodynamic understanding as the patient gains insight into thoughts, feelings and fantasies that trigger various difficulties.

A Brief Clinical Example

A retired woman in her 60s presented for treatment when she became depressed after taking on major responsibilities in a family business and entered PrFPP. She felt trapped by the workload and resentful toward a relative who expected her to handle many administrative tasks. Yet she felt unable to reduce her responsibilities or challenge the arrangement.

In therapy, it became clear that she associated disengaging from responsibilities with being “lazy” and “selfish.” In exploring the origins of her difficulties, therapist and patient learned that during her adolescence, when her mother became seriously ill, she had been expected to assume substantial household duties. When she protested, she felt criticized by her father and experienced guilt. Years later, she still expected other people to condemn her if she felt overwhelmed and refused a task. Therapist and patient were able to identify feelings of anger about these demands, which triggered further guilt and shame.

Her therapist helped her connect these earlier experiences with her current situation and recognize how guilt about anger made it difficult to assert herself. She began speaking more directly with family members about how she felt overwhelmed by these tasks. Some were far more understanding than she had expected. Eventually, these changes enabled her to step away from the business, and her depressive symptoms substantially improved. She also became more alert to taking on unnecessary obligations in other areas of her life.

Insight and Change Can Work Together

Psychodynamic therapists do not have to choose between understanding behavior and changing it. In PrFPP, the two processes often strengthen each other. Identifying factors that contribute to a behavior can determine interventions that better enable change to occur. Trying a new behavior, in turn, can expose fears, guilt, assumptions, and conflicts that were previously difficult to access, enabling further work on those issues.
